title: The Hoofers today and what tap's future holds
summary: The interviewer lists the dead and the Hoofers today, and Green hopes new academies will make the Hoofers' legacy last.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well, Chuck, I know that many of your colleagues, many of the pioneers of this era passed away. Baby Lawrence passed away; Pete Nugent; Buddy Bradley.
I know that people like Rhythm Red, Derby Wilson aren't tapping any longer.
So, today I know that there is a group, the Hoofers, that you are the senior member of. Sandman Sims, Raymond Kailen, Jimmy Sly, Harold Kromer, Bernard Manners, the youngest member of the group.

And you're still performing together, still performing the similar routines except for more refined, and it's representative of the whole eras -- all the eras of tap dancing in your show. Tell me a little bit about that and what's happening with it today. And what you feel about tap dancing and its -- what you see for it in the future.
Well, I must go along with the majority

here, and I think the Hoofers will be like scratch rock was to the Injuns. I mean forever and a day we can say. Because there's going to be new academies, I think, erected in the future, which is the greatest schools we would ever have. And they're going to be either the contracted or employed to reissue the classes, see. Because (unintelligible) the child I think I could say. I think that's what the Hoofers are. Well, at least some of them. Maybe the elders or the younger ones, you know. Youngsters -- that's what they would like to happen.
